Which of the following statements are true regarding the graph of the function $y=f(x)$ shown above? 

I. ${lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(-2+h)-f(-2)}{h}=1$

II. ${lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(h)-f(0)}{h}=-0.5$

III. ${lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(-3+h)-f(-3)}{h}=1$
question.worked_solution:
Comparing these limits with the formula for the instantaneous rate of change

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h},
$$

we see that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(-2+h)-f(-2)}{h} & ={f}^{′}(-2), \\ {lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(h)-f(0)}{h} & ={f}^{′}(0), \\ {lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(-3+h)-f(-3)}{h} & ={f}^{′}(-3).\end{aligned}
$$

The function consists of three line segments. Inspecting the graph, we see that

- for $x<-1$, we have  ${f}^{′}(x)=1,$

- for $-1<x<1$, we have  ${f}^{′}(x)=-1,$

- for $x>1$, we have  ${f}^{′}(x)=1.$

The derivative does not exist at $x=-1$ and $x=1$ . So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(-2+h)-f(-2)}{h} & =1, \\ {lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(h)-f(0)}{h} & =-1, \\ {lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(-3+h)-f(-3)}{h} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, only I and III are true.
